title: Waste Collection Company Feels Contract Pressure Amid Diesel Price Hike
seoTitle: Waste Collection Company Struggles with Diesel Price Hike
subtitle: Long-term contracts prevent quick tariff adjustments despite surging fuel prices
excerpt: JLT Trucking, operating over 100 trucks in the Washington and Baltimore area, reports a nearly 60% diesel price increase is costing them approximately $100,000 monthly.
author: Daniele Morais
sourceName: ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
contentHtml:
The abrupt increase in diesel prices is forcing JLT Trucking to absorb costs reaching up to $100,000 per month, according to its market development director. This situation has raised concerns about the viability of maintaining waste collection services.

Long-term Contracts and Rising Diesel Costs

According to Marc Shaener, long-term agreements with clients make it difficult to quickly raise tariffs. He states that the company cannot adjust prices at the same speed as the fuel increase.

Financial Impact on the Fleet

Shaener reports that the fleet, consisting of over 100 trucks, consumes approximately 2,000 gallons of diesel per day. The projected additional expenditure reaches $1.2 million annually, reflecting a nearly 60% price increase since the start of the conflict involving Iran.

External Causes of Price Increase

The average price of diesel reached a record $6.49 per gallon, according to GasBuddy, driven by clashes between Houthis and Saudi Arabia and the war between Iran and Ukraine, which affect international energy transport.

Repercussions for Collection Operations

Shaener warns that when costs rise, waste collection is the first to feel the impact, as clients need to cut expenses. He emphasizes that the company must communicate the situation to clients, employees, and investors, as financial pressure can reduce investments and affect the workforce.

Tariff Adjustment Outlook

Although contracts provide for annual or quinquennial adjustments, the speed of the diesel price hike prevents JLT from immediately passing on costs. Shaener indicates that, with no relief in sight, the company may face a decrease in business and the need to review its pricing strategies in the future.
